paper_title: Not All Objectives Are Born Equal: Priority-Constrained Descent for Hierarchical Multi-Objective Optimization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Deep learning problems rarely involve objectives that are equal in importance. A primary objective defines the goal, whilst secondary objectives, such as sparsity, compression, or robustness constrain the solution. While existing multi-objective methods have proven effective in practice, they have a clear symmetry problem and neglect the inherent objective hierarchy built into these objective spaces. We introduce Priority-Constrained Descent (PCD), a gradient-based optimization framework designed to explicitly exploit hierarchical objective structures. PCD preserves the direction of primary descent whilst allowing for the minimal distortion necessary to guarantee progress on secondary objectives, controlled by a single $τ\in [0, 1]$ that dictates the strength of the distortion. The resulting formulation is invariant to objective scaling and admits exact closed-form solutions for problems with two and three objectives. We evaluate PCD within structured network compression settings, unstructured sparsity and low-rankness, and across a variety of synthetic experiments, showing Pareto dominance and better per-objective performance with secondary progress guarantees over existing methods, further exhibiting the interpretable trade-off that $τ$ provides.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Optimization in modern deep learning is fundamentally hierarchical. While models are typically evaluated based on their primary objective performance (such as accuracy in the case of classification, mean squared error for regression, or fidelity for generative modeling), solutions often need to satisfy number of secondary conditions to be usable in practice. In the case of pruning, the primary task loss is paired with sparsityinducing regularizer that heavily constrains the final parameterization (He & Xiao, 2023). Low-rankness pairs the primary objective with rank-constraining regularizer to force the network parameters into lowdimensional subspace (Idelbayev & Carreira-Perpinán, 2020). Quantization-aware training anchors the task against fidelity term penalizing drift from discrete values (Abushahla et al., 2025). Similarly, continual learning balances fitness on new data against replay objective preserving past knowledge (Wang et al., 2024), while federated learning manages local accuracy alongside communication constraints (Zhang et al., 2021). In all these examples, the structure of the optimization problem is the same: the relationship between objectives is asymmetric by design. One loss represents the core capability, while the others dictate the boundaries within which that capability must be learned. Nonetheless, standard multi-objective optimization (MOO) frameworks ignore this structural truth. The conventional paradigm for handling multiple objectives is to collapse all objectives into single weighted summation = wiLi (Marler & Arora, 2010). Here, importance is encoded implicitly through the weights wi, but this requires fragile hyperparameter sweeps and struggles to access non-convex regions of the Pareto front. Gradient-based methods (Désidéri, 2009; Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021a; 2023) avoid these pitfalls 1 Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (09/2026) Figure 1: PCD on 2D toy problem with two local minima of L1, only one of which is also minimum of L2. From three initializations, weighted sum, MGDA, PCGrad, CAGrad, and FAMO all terminate at Pareto-stationary point at which L2 remains non-zero (the conflict equilibrium of Sec. 3). From all three initializations, PCD crosses the saddle barrier in parameter space and reaches the composite bi-stationary point where L1 = L2 = 0, which is minimizer for both L1 and L2. but share the issue of treating objectives symmetrically. Consequently, they target Pareto stationarity, where no objective can be improved without harming others. For hierarchical problems, we argue that this is too restrictive criterion. It can lead to what we term conflict equilibrium, sub-optimal state where progress on the primary objective is halted because its gradient is counterbalanced by the push-back of constraints with equal authority (formalized in Sec. 3). This is failure mode and not feasible solution for practitioners. What hierarchical optimization problems call for is an optimizer that imposes priority at the gradient level, avoiding the issue of halting prematurely by overly enforcing secondary objectives. To this end, we introduce Priority-Constrained Descent (PCD), framework designed to follow the primary gradient as closely as possible, deflecting only as much as necessary to keep secondary objectives on track. single scalar tolerance τ [0, 1] controls this deflection. Three outcomes follow from this design (developed in Sec. 4): first, the update anchors to the primary task and reduces to plain gradient descent whenever primary descent alone provides enough progress on all secondaries (Cor. 4.3). Second, every step guarantees τ -fraction of firstorder progress on each secondary for the direction it computes (Prop. 4.4), and third, the normalized update direction vanishes only at composite multi-stationary (CMS) points, strictly stronger condition than Pareto stationarity. At CMS points, every objective is individually stationary (Thm. 4.8), so conflict equilibria are never fixed points of the PCD direction. This geometric advantage is immediately visible in 2D landscape  (Fig. 1)  . When faced with saddle barrier separating local and global minimum, all symmetric baselines stall at Pareto-stationary conflict equilibrium where L2 remains non-zero. PCD is the only method tested that pushes through the secondary constraints to reach the composite bi-stationary point where L1 = L2 = 0, successfully minimizing both 2 Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (09/2026) objectives. We note that although L1 comes close to (but never truly reaches) 0, PCD continues to explore the combined landscape until both objectives are minimized. We summarize the core contributions of this study as follows: Priority-Constrained Descent: gradient-based optimizer that solves small convex quadratic program (QP) to minimally distort the primary gradient, enabling progress for the primary objective whilst guaranteeing first-order progress on secondaries for the direction it computes. The anchoredprojection construction follows the established dynamic-barrier algorithm of Gong et al. (2021) and Ye & Liu (2022) whilst expanding to per-objective, scale-normalized margins that make one dimensionless tolerance meaningful across heterogeneous secondaries. We derive exact closed-form solutions for 2 and 3 objectives, feasibility characterization at general K, asymptotic invariance to per-objective scaling, and the fixed-point analysis of the resulting update. Structured Network Compression: We show the dominance of PCD over existing MOO frameworks across variety of architectures and datasets for structured pruning tasks, showing minimal drop in accuracy compared to unpruned baselines. On CIFAR-100 trained on the ResNet-34 architecture, PCD maintains 70.9% accuracy at 90% sparsity (compared to an unpruned initial accuracy of 73.3%), where baselines collapse. Against tuned pruning-specific and constrained baselines, PCD exceeds accuracy at matched sparsity throughout the compression regime, with other comparisons coming within seed noise. Unstructured Pruning and Low-Rankness: On the tri-objective task with ℓ1 and nuclear norms, PCD is decisive on two of the three axes and is competitive on the third, maintaining accuracies of 71% for CIFAR-100 trained on ResNet-34 with an unstructured sparsity of 92.6% and an effective rank of 24.5, whilst baselines once again collapse in terms of accuracy and over-compress. Synthetic Verification: In known objective spaces, we verify the mechanisms of PCD directly, showing asymptotic scale invariance, feasibility as we increase the number of objectives, and the fixed-point separation from symmetric methods. We observe empirically that PCD reaches CMS points in all cases without infeasibility issues.

sections.title: 2 Related Works
sections.content: Modern gradient-based MOO rests on target established by Gale et al. (1951). point θ is Pareto stationary if the origin lies in the convex hull of the objective gradients, meaning no common descent direction exists. Traditional MOO frameworks aim at reaching Pareto-stationary point, with more nuanced techniques allowing for some degree of preference over the Pareto front itself. In the pursuit of Pareto stationarity, the field has branched into two distinct strategies: scalarization and direct gradient manipulation. Classical weighted-sum scalarization (Marler & Arora, 2010) collapses the objective space prior to optimization. While any stationary point with strictly positive weights (assigned to each objective) is technically Pareto stationary, this approach cannot reach non-convex regions of the Pareto front (Miettinen, 1999) and requires brittle hyperparameter tuning. recent study reports that well-tuned weighted sum frequently matches the performance of more elaborate alternatives, suggesting that the gains attributed to complex MOO algorithms are often artifacts of the training process rather than fundamental algorithmic superiority (Xin et al., 2022). Regardless, to bypass these pathologies, Fliege & Svaiter (2000) proposed second strategy: discarding scalar weights entirely to compute the steepest Pareto-descent direction directly from the gradients. Nearly every modern gradient-based MOO method inherits this direct-direction strategy. However, while they successfully escape scale sensitivity and access broader regions of the Pareto front, they preserve structural assumption that contradicts the reality of hierarchical deep learning: that objectives are symmetric and inherently interchangeable. In Pursuit of Symmetric Compromise. The direct-direction lineage largely stems from MGDA (Désidéri, 2009), which operationalizes Pareto stationarity by identifying the minimum-norm element of the gradients convex hull. Sener & Koltun (2018) scaled MGDA to deep learning via FrankWolfe solver 3 Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (09/2026) (Jaggi, 2013), while MoCo (Fernando et al., 2023; 2024) mitigated the gradient bias inherent to stochastic MGDA variants, recovering provable convergence in non-convex settings. In parallel, separate family of methods takes the gradients as given and attempts to condition them before they are combined. Magnitudebased approaches balance objectives by scaling losses via learned homoscedastic noise (Kendall et al., 2018), driving gradient norms to common rate (Chen et al., 2018), ensuring equal gradient projections (Liu et al., 2021b), or tracking loss histories to balance step decreases (Liu et al., 2023). Geometry-based approaches attempt to resolve gradient misalignment by projecting conflicting task gradients onto each others normal planes (Yu et al., 2020), or by finding an optimal direction within an averaged-gradient ball (Liu et al., 2021a; Senushkin et al., 2023). However, even when methods attempt to prioritize certain outcomes, they do so symmetrically. Preferencesteering methods like EPO (Mahapatra & Rajan, 2021), PMGDA (Zhang et al., 2025), and hypernetwork adaptations (Navon et al., 2020) target specific Pareto-optimal points via controlled ascent or test-time network mapping. Yet, the preference vector enters these formulations as symmetric annotation on the objectives, not as structural distinction. Across all these methods, whether modifying directions, magnitudes, or geometries, the fundamental goal is compromise. As noted earlier, enforcing this symmetric compromise in hierarchical settings is precisely what traps optimizers in sub-optimal conflict equilibria. Breaking The Symmetry. The shift away from symmetric MOO has begun to surface in recent gametheoretic and constrained-optimization literature. Nash MTL (Navon et al., 2022) applies the Nash Bargaining solution to produce proportionally fair update directions. Building on this, AuxiNash (Shamsian et al., 2023) marks critical conceptual pivot: it extends Nash-MTL to asymmetric settings by learning task-specific bargaining power based on each auxiliarys contribution to the primary objective. It explicitly names the limitation that symmetric methods treat structurally unequal objectives as peers. Similarly, constrained-optimization frameworks like Cooper (Gallego-Posada et al., 2025) establish hierarchy through Lagrangian multiplier dynamics, updating learned dual variables alongside primal parameters. Anchored Projections and Dynamic Barriers. Closest to our construction is the family of methods that anchor on one gradient and impose inner-product constraints on others. Dynamic Barrier Gradient Descent (DBGD; Gong et al., 2021) is PCDs = 2 instance on raw gradients, developed for constrained and lexicographic optimization with convergence guarantees in the raw-gradient setting. Pareto Navigation Gradient Descent (Ye & Liu, 2022) similarly introduces an anchored program with general objectives, with shared and scheduled approach rather than per-objective margins. Within the field of continual learning, methods such as GEM (Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017) and A-GEM (Chaudhry et al., 2019) have been developed to combat catastrophic forgetting, but are algorithmically equivalent to PCD with τ = 0. ε-SOFT-GEM (Hu et al., 2020) adds unit-normalized positive margin at = 2 in the same continuallearning setting, while on the application side Gallego-Posada et al. (2022) make the argument closest to ours, controlling the compression level directly rather than tuning penalty coefficient, via constrained L0 sparsity. Within this line, PCD contributes the per-objective scale-normalized margins that make single dimensionless parameter τ meaningful across variety of applications. While AuxiNash and Cooper recognize the asymmetric reality of modern deep learning, and anchored projection methods present application-specific alternatives, they enforce hierarchy through learned bargaining weights, Lagrangian dynamics, or by exploiting application-specific mechanisms. PCD discards the symmetry assumption at much lower level. Rather than relying on learned coefficients, PCD embeds hierarchy directly into the geometry of the update. By calculating the closed-form Euclidean projection of the primary gradient onto the secondary-progress polyhedron, PCD yields per-step first-order progress guarantee on secondary objectives for the direction it feeds the optimizer (Sec. 4.7). It fundamentally rejects the symmetric compromise of Pareto stationarity: the fixed points of its normalized direction are composite multi-stationary rather than merely Pareto stationary (Sec. 4.8). 4 Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (09/2026)

sections.title: 4 Priority-Constrained Descent
sections.content: Based on the principle of anchoring to the primary gradient and admitting corrections along the secondaries to ensure progress, we now present the algorithmic framework for PCD. This framing of corrections should be carefully defined: in Euclidean distance, it is simply the resultant direction that lies as close as possible to the primary gradient vector. Coupled with the role of the tolerance parameter τ [0, 1], we formalize the PCD update rule in this section. The development proceeds as follows: Sec. 4.1 states the QP and identifies its solution as the Euclidean projection of the primary gradient onto polyhedron of secondary-progress 5 Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (09/2026) half-spaces. Sec. 4.2 extracts the KKT identity that makes the asymmetric structure of the update explicit, and Sec. 4.3 draws the per-step secondary-progress guarantee directly from it. Sec. 4.4 then introduces the gradient normalization that gives τ scale-invariant interpretation across objectives of vastly different magnitude. Sec. 4.5 specializes to two objectives, where the QP admits closed-form solution and τ geometric meaning becomes quantitative through an analytical threshold at which primary descent breaks down, and Sec. 4.6 states the full algorithm. Sec. 4.7 delimits the scope of the guarantees, and Sec. 4.8 closes with the endpoint characterization of the normalized direction, under which conflict equilibria are not fixed points. Comparison with existing gradient-based MOO methods is deferred to Sec. 4.9.

sections.content: In this section, we conduct experiments over two application domains and one set of synthetic experiments to demonstrate the superiority of PCD in asymmetric applications. In particular, we conduct experiments involving structured pruning and compression of neural networks (Sec. 5.1) with = 2 objectives, unstructured sparse and low-rank networks (Sec. 5.2) with = 3 objectives, and set of synthetic experiments to validate PCDs advantages (Sec. 5.3). 5.1 Structured Pruning Structured neural-network compression is natural instance of asymmetric multi-objective optimization. We set the primary objective L1 to be the standard cross-entropy loss and the secondary objective L2 to be the Group Lasso penalty: L2(θ) = θg2, (18) Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (09/2026) where the sum runs over groups defined at the output-channel level of each layer. The formulation is asymmetric by construction: task accuracy is the deliverable, while structural sparsity is secondary objective whose pressure is controlled by τ . After training, groups whose norm θg2 falls below threshold are removed and the resulting network is evaluated directly without fine-tuning. To produce results at specified parameter-reduction target {80%, 85%, 90%, 95%, 99%}, the threshold is selected post hoc, per (method, architecture, dataset, target), as the smallest value for which the fraction of removed parameters reaches r. Why Group Lasso? Group Lasso (Yuan & Lin, 2006) penalizes defined groups of parameters so that entire groups are driven to zero, rather than individual weights. With each group set to one output channel, group at zero is removable filter: removal yields smaller dense network that runs on standard hardware with no sparse kernels, no special runtime, and no change of format. Channel-level Group Lasso is the standard regularizer for exactly this reason. Wen et al. (2016) introduced it as Structured Sparsity Learning, and Liu et al. (2017) apply the same principle in Network Slimming. This choice makes our secondary objective comparable to that line of work rather than to unstructured magnitude pruning (Han et al., 2015). It is also what makes the deployment measurements below meaningful: FLOPs, latency, and file size in Tables 1 and 2 are measured on CPU inference after removing the zeroed filters, with no fine-tuning and no sparse kernels. An unstructured penalty would not permit that measurement. 5.1.1 Comparison with General Multi-Objective Methods Experimental Protocol. We evaluate on four architectures spanning range of structural properties: DenseNet-121 (Huang et al., 2017), ResNet-34 (He et al., 2016), an Inception-style model (Szegedy et al., 2015), and MobileNetV2 (Howard et al., 2017; Sandler et al., 2018), each trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR100 (Krizhevsky et al., 2009). All models are trained from scratch with Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2014), learning rate 103, batch size 128, cosine annealing, and 300 epochs. Each configuration is run for 5 independent seeds, with the reported numbers being means. PCD is compared against six multi-objective baselines: PCGrad, MGDA, FAMO, CAGrad, weighted sum (WS), and AuxiNash. For baselines with tunable hyperparameter (the weight for WS, the conflict coefficient for CAGrad, and for AuxiNash), we sweep over {0.1, 0.2, . . . , 0.9} and report the best operating point per configuration. MGDA, PCGrad, and FAMO have no such hyperparameter and are run at their default settings. For PCD we use denser τ sweep {0.01, 0.02, . . . , 0.09, 0.1, 0.2, . . . , 0.9, 1}. DBGD also serves as the representative of the lexicographic family: its lexicographic convergence analysis concerns exactly the update evaluated here, and Cooper covers the constrained route. The comparison is restricted to trainingtime, native-sparsity methods under one identical protocol. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Multi-objective optimization in deep learning has long been limited in its applications by an artificial symmetry. By treating primary tasks and secondary constraints as equals, standard MOO methods routinely trap optimization trajectories in conflict equilibria. Priority-Constrained Descent (PCD) dismantles this symmetry. By anchoring updates to the primary gradient and admitting only the minimal Euclidean distortion necessary to maintain first-order secondary progress, PCD enforces its constraints on the direction it computes without sacrificing the primary deliverable. Governed by single, interpretable scalar τ , the framework is asymptotically scale-invariant, admits exact closed-form solutions for practical objective counts, and its normalized direction vanishes only at composite multi-stationary points, with the deployed-update caveats stated in Sec. 4.7. As demonstrated across neural network compression (against both general multi-objective 24 Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (09/2026) methods and tuned pruning-specific baselines) and synthetic experiments, PCD provides what hierarchical pipelines demand: stable, controllable trade-off curve that consistently outperforms symmetric baselines at matched compression. The theoretical guarantees of PCD rely on secondary objectives being proper, convex, and lower semicontinuous. Consequently, inherently non-convex constraints such as adversarial losses or hard combinatorial sparsity targets fall outside our formal geometric proofs, which apply locally to the normalized first-order step. Extending the convergence guarantees known for the raw-gradient dynamic-barrier update (Gong et al., 2021) to the normalized, stochastic update deployed here remains open. Furthermore, while the composite multi-stationarity theorem characterizes the exact fixed-point structure of the deterministic update, the underlying quadratic program could theoretically become infeasible for > 2 if the secondary constraints are strictly and mutually incompatible. Although Sec. 5.3 demonstrates this to be improbable, we note it as possible limitation regardless. While our synthetic experiments probe the feasibility of the constraint polyhedron up to = 8 and compare against traditional MOO baselines for {2, . . . , 7}, we note that typical asymmetric optimization applications rarely necessitate such large number of distinct objectives in practice. PCD establishes foundation for hierarchical optimization, opening several immediate avenues for extension. The most direct is the development of adaptive τ schedules, which would dynamically anneal constraint strength based on the training trajectory or current feasibility (as outlined in App. B.1). Beyond the strict primarysecondary dichotomy, extending the formulation to multi-level priority hierarchies where an arbitrary number of objectives are strictly ordered with distinct, cascading tolerances offers natural mathematical next step. More broadly, the per-objective tolerances of Remark B.1 trace (K1)-dimensional operating manifold within the tolerance hypercube [0, 1]K1, of which scalar τ is the diagonal slice and cascading hierarchies an ordered sub-family. The open challenge is recovering this expressiveness by setting the τj adaptively or via learned criterion, rather than by exponential grid search over the cube, so that PCDs single-knob interpretability is extended rather than spent. On the application side, deploying PCD under strict, hardware-aware constraints, or adapting it for structured generative modeling where primary output fidelity must survive heavy structural regularizers, represents highly promising frontier for the framework. sections.content: Proposition 4.4 concerns the direction handed to the optimizer. Adams diagonal preconditioner and momentum do not need to preserve the sign of gj, θ for the realized step θ (Sec. 4.7). We measure this directly: at every optimizer step of 3-seed runs on two configurations and two tolerances, we log the sign-flip fraction (steps where signg2, θ signg2, d), the alignment the QP promises (cos(g2, d)), and the alignment the optimizer realizes (cos(g2, θ)), under the deployed Adam and under an SGD-withmomentum (0.9) control. Under the deployed Adam optimizer, the per-step sign survives on 92.399.8% of steps, and the realized alignment with the secondary is at least 5 stronger than the QPs guaranteed margin (comparing the last two columns of Table 18). In this regime, Adam amplifies rather than erodes the constraint. Under SGD with momentum, the buffer dwarfs the small guaranteed margin τ g22 and the per-step sign flips on 47 73% of steps, with realized alignment 0. sections.title: H Reproducibility Details
sections.content: All runs in this paper use Adam as the default optimizer (unless otherwise stated), with β1 = 0.9 and β2 = 0.999. The default learning rate used was 103, batch size of 128, cosine annealing, and everything was trained for 300 epochs. No warm-up (training pure cross-entropy) nor any weight decay was used. PCDs own constants are the EMA normalization used β = 0.999 with bias correction, and solver stabilizer of ε = 108. 5 seeds are used throughout the paper unless otherwise stated (3 in the case of the ablations). Operating points shown in figures are selected based on mean test accuracy: each swept baseline is reported at its highest mean test accuracy, and we use fixed τ = 0.02 as representative, unless otherwise stated or swept. No held-out validation split was used. Seed standard deviations accompany every table of the tuned baseline study (App. E.4), the normalization grid (App. E.1), and every cell of the = 3 operating-point table  (Table 15)  . For Table 5, PCDs accuracy standard deviation is 0.150.40 across the four configurations while the baselines average 1.26 with maximum of 6.14 (MGDA, ResNet-34/CIFAR-10).
